# Achieving 30 by 30

Last updated: 27 March 2026

**On this page**

* Protecting and conserving 30% of marine areas
* Protecting and conserving 30% of land
* National roadmap for protecting and conserving 30% of Australia’s land by 2030
* Building Australia’s Conserved Area Network
* Protecting Important Biodiversity Areas Program
* Australian Bushland Program
* Private land conservation

The Australian Government has set a national target to protect and conserve 30% of Australia’s landmass and 30% of Australia’s marine areas by 2030 (the ‘30 by 30’ target).

This aligns with Target 3 of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (GBF) under the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD).

In October 2022, environment ministers agreed to work together to reach the national 30 by 30 target.

See the Environment Ministers Meeting – 21 October 2022 agreed communiqué (PDF 167.32 KB) | (DOCX 25.07 KB)

## Protecting and conserving 30% of marine areas

Australia has one of the world’s largest representative systems of marine protected areas .

Our marine protected areas cover 52% of Australian waters. That's 4.6 million square kilometres. About 24% of our waters, or 2.
2 million square kilometres, are in highly protected ‘no-take’ areas.

Australia’s marine protected areas cover vast ocean areas that are important to:

* conserve biodiversity
* support the sustainable management of our marine resources
* protect our natural and cultural heritage.

In June 2025, the Environment Minister committed to ensuring 30% of Australia’s marine environment is highly protected by 2030.

The Australian Government manages [Australian Marine Parks (external link)](https://australianmarineparks.gov.au/) in accordance with statutory management plans. These set out the management arrangements for the parks. This includes zoning arrangements and their associated levels of protection.

We are reviewing 5 of these plans, covering 44 marine parks. The reviews are an important opportunity to meet the 30% highly protected target.

## Protecting and conserving 30% of land

The National Reserve System (NRS) is Australia’s network of protected land areas.

...

Conserved areas provide conservation in places where formal protection is:

* not possible
* not appropriate, or
* not supported.

The framework supports a nationally consistent approach by:

* setting out principles to guide the recognition of conserved areas
* providing information on implementation of the principles
* providing a site assessment tool that landholders can use to determine if their land meets the requirements for a conserved area.

Governments are implementing the framework gradually. We have begun with a small number of pilot projects.

Read more about Australia’s Conserved Area Network of Other Effective area-based Conservation Measures (OECMs) .

## Protecting Important Biodiversity Areas Program

We are investing $25 million in the Protecting Important Biodiversity Areas Program. This supports initiatives to protect and conserve our land.

The program invests in projects that will:

* grow protected areas
* trial arrangements to recognise conserved areas
* leverage investment to protect important biodiversity areas, including on private land
* contribute to the target to protect and conserve 30% of Australia’s land by 2030.

The first 2 projects under the program are underway.

We have invested $1.5 million to expand [critical habitat in Victoria (external link)](https://minister.dcceew.gov.au/plibersek/media-releases/25-million-better-protect-nature) . This includes protecting high-quality remnant vegetation in the Victorian Riverina's grasslands. The area is important habitat for threatened species, including the critically endangered Plains-wanderer. We are partnering with:

* the Victorian Government
* Trust for Nature (Victoria)
* the Nature Conservancy
* Country Road and other private sector sponsors.

We have invested $3 million to expand the [Nature Refuge footprint across Queensland (external link)](https://minister.dcceew.gov.
au/plibersek/media-releases/joint-media-release-far-north-queensland-biodiversity-secured-thanks-new-protected-areas) , in partnership with the Queensland Government. This includes:

* expanding the Crystalvale Nature Refuge in Far North Queensland
* establishing the Abingdon Downs Nature Refuge in Far North Queensland.

## Australian Bushland Program

The Australian Government announced the Australian Bushland Program in March 2025. This program provides $250 million over five years to protect and conserve more of Australia’s environment and progress the 30 by 30 target.

## Private land conservation

Around 60% of Australia’s land is privately owned or managed.

Private land conservation has the potential to contribute to the 30 by 30 land target. Currently, less than 6% of Australia’s protected areas are on private land.

Landowners can apply a conservation covenant over all, or part of, their property.

# What’s in the 2025-26 federal budget for nature?

## Back to more news

## News story

## 1 April 2025

## The federal budget was released on Tuesday 25 March. We have examined it with a fine-tooth comb to see what it held for nature. Here are some of our insights:

#### Small bump in biodiversity investment for the election but longer-term declines

The budget for on-ground biodiversity programs equates to 0.06% of the total Federal budget for 2025-56.

Spending on on-ground biodiversity programs is up 7.2% for 2025-26 ($474.1M) compared to the last financial year ($442.3M). However, it is forecast that this will drop down $92.6M (-19.5% to $381.6M) in 2026-27 and remain at this level (+1% to $384.5M) in 2027-28. So it is a temporary bump in an election year.

The largest single source of funding for on-ground biodiversity programs is the [Natural Heritage Trust](https://www.dcceew.gov.au/environment/land/natural-heritage-trust) accounting for over half of all spending ($213.
9M per year) from 2025-26 to 2028-29. The budget papers do not enable a program or project level breakdown of the funding, but large investments include Indigenous Protected Areas, threatened species and priority landscapes, and urban rivers and catchments.

Expenditure of on-ground biodiversity programs

#### Growing the area of conservation land was the single headline investment

Investment to expand Australia’s conservation reserves network was the main item to receive substantial new funding, with $250M committed over the next five years delivered through a new Australian Bushland Program.

This is a small step toward delivering Australia’s commitment under the Global Biodiversity Framework to conserve 30 per cent of its lands by 2030. It’s [estimated](https://report.30by30.org.au/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2023/11/Report3030_FINAL_web-1.
pdf) that 20 times that amount is needed to deliver the full commitment of a connected and protected area network that represents all key ecosystems.

Funding for the establishment of this program was partly offset by the end of other nature-focused programs.

#### Threatened species investment is still inadequate to prevent extinctions and recovery species

Australia has more than 2000 threatened species. The only species to get a substantial new investment to fund its conservation in this budget was the Maugean skate ($27.7M over 4 years). Another notable investment was in preparing for Avian Influenza H5N1 for priority native species, which amounted to $6.4M in 2024-25 and $22.4M in 2025-26.

Most of Australia’s threatened species continue to receive little to no investment in their protection and recovery. In fact, resourcing for the Saving Native Species Fund has been reduced from $63.1M in 2024-25 to $38.3M in 2025-26, with no funding beyond that.
In October 2022, Minister Plibersek [announced](https://minister.dcceew.gov.au/plibersek/media-releases/minister-launches-threatened-species-action-plan-toward-zero-extinctions) the Saving Native Species Fund Program with a commitment to spending $224.5M over 4 years. That was the number in the media announcements

What is also surprising, given the chronic shortage of funds for conservation action for most threatened species is that there were large underspends of allocated funding in the Saving Native Species Program in its first two years, (underspent by $16.8M in 2022-23 and by $26.7M in 2023-24) and the underspend was not carried forward as usually occurs. Once forecast spending for this year is included, the program will spend a total of $161.1M over 4 years before it ends in 2025-26. This is $63.4M or 28% less than originally committed to.

Forecast and actual spending on the Saving Native Species Program

...

Overall, investment in caring for nature, like recovering threatened species, controlling feral animals and weeds, and better managing fires, is still less than one-thousandth of the federal budget.

The funding allocated to nature-related programs in the 2025-26 federal budget is not adequate to deliver the Australian Government’s own environmental commitments to prevent extinctions of plants and animals, restore degraded lands and conserve 30% of lands and seas by 2023.

Lifting nature’s share of the federal budget to just 1% would provide enough funding to meet most of the Australian Government’s environmental commitments. Recent research undertaken by Monash University for the Biodiversity Council found that most Australians believe that at least 1% of the federal budget should be dedicated to nature protection.

See our analysis of Federal Government spending on nature-related programs.
[Analysis of Federal Government spending on nature-related programs](https://biodiversitycouncil.org.au/resources/federal-government-spending-on-nature-related-programs)

#### Methodology

The Biodiversity Council reviewed the Portfolio Budget Statements of the Department of Climate Change, Energy, Environment and Water (DCCEEW) and the Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry (DAFF) to identify nature-related programs.

The following programs have been categorised as ‘on-ground biodiversity programs’: the Natural Heritage Trust, Saving Native Species, Australian Bushland Program, Environmental Stewardship Program, Maugean Skate Conservation and Recovery, Avian Influenza Preparedness Program, Great Barrier Reef Leadership and Stewardship Program, Reef Trust Programs, Australian Marine Parks and the Oceans Leadership Programs. Funding for these programs can be found in the [2025-26 DCCEEW Portfolio Budget paper](https://www.dcceew.gov.

## About the framework

In June 2024, Environment Ministers agreed to the National Other Effective area-based Conservation Measures (OECM) Framework. This framework enables the recognition of land-based OECMs in Australia, referred to as Conserved Areas.

Conserved Areas can contribute to our national target to protect and conserve 30% of land by 2030. Conserved Areas provide conservation in places where formal protection is not:

* possible
* appropriate
* supported.

The framework supports a nationally consistent approach by:

* identifying principles to guide Conserved Area recognition
* providing information on implementation of these principles
* including a site assessment tool for landholders. The tool is used to determine whether a site meets the requirements for a Conserved Area.

This framework sets out a new approach to the conservation of biodiversity in Australia.

## About the site assessment tool

To assess your site for potential eligibility as a Conserved Area, please complete the site assessment tool and return to NRS.environment@dcceew.gov.au . Please note your information will be provided to the relevant state or territory government. Your information will be used by us and the relevant state or territory government for assessment, review, approval and reporting processes.

# Australia’s National Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plan

Last updated: 27 March 2026
In December 2022, the 15th meeting of the Conference of Parties to the United Nations Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) was held. Australia was one of 188 countries to adopt the [Kunming Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (external link)](https://www.cbd.int/gbf) (the GBF).

The GBF aims to:

* halt and reverse biodiversity loss by 2030
* live in harmony with nature by 2050.

The GBF has 23 targets to achieve by 2030 and 4 goals to achieve by 2050.

Parties to the CBD agreed to update their National Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plans. Updated plans may also include national targets to support the GBF.

## Australia’s Strategy for Nature

Our National Biodiversity Strategy and Action plan is called Australia’s Strategy for Nature 2024–2030 . It sets national targets in 6 priority areas of the Global Biodiversity Framework. These are most important to reducing biodiversity loss in Australia between now and 2030.

The strategy also identifies 3 enablers of change.
These will help us to:

* achieve transformational change
* deliver results that meet the targets.

They recognise the broader effort required to support our ability to protect our biodiversity.

The Strategy for Nature is a shared roadmap. It helps us to:

* better understand
* care for
* sustainably manage nature.

Read Australia’s Strategy for Nature 2024-2030

### Implementation Plan

On 27 March 2026, environment ministers agreed the Strategy’s implementation plan. It sets out how we will halt and reverse biodiversity loss by 2030.

The plan guides joint action from:

* governments
* First Nations peoples
* business
* non-government organisations
* academic and research organisations
* communities.

The plan:

* highlights work supporting Australia’s 6 targets and 3 enablers of change
* identifies areas where more work is needed
* outlines our approach to monitoring and reporting.

The plan was developed by the Australian and state and territory governments.
It incorporates input from:

* First Nations peoples
* the public
* environmental organisations
* the scientific community
* industry.

Read more: Australia’s Strategy for Nature 2024-2030: Implementation Plan

### National biodiversity targets

Environment ministers agreed to national environmental targets . These support the Global Biodiversity Framework as part of the Strategy for Nature.

#### Protect and conserve 30% of Australia's landmass and 30% of Australia's marine areas by 2030

This target aims to:

* protect and conserve at least 30% of Australia’s terrestrial and inland water areas, and marine and coastal areas by 2030, especially areas of particular importance for biodiversity and ecosystem functions and services
* ensure protected and conserved areas are ecologically representative, well-connected and effectively managed, recognising and respecting the rights of First Nation peoples.

This target aligns with GBF Target 3.
